opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #1061: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős asked how many pairs a, b with a + b at most x satisfy sigma(a) + sigma(b) = sigma(a+b), and whether the count is about a constant times x. In June 2026 Eric Li posted a paper claiming the count exceeds x times any fixed power of log x, which answers the dichotomy in the higher-order direction. There is no Lean development, so nothing here can be settled by a rerun; the first thing owed is a formal deduction or an independent reading. Everything here is open.

background.spoken: Let sigma(n) be the sum of the divisors of n. Count the pairs of positive integers a, b with a + b at most x such that sigma(a) + sigma(b) = sigma(a + b). Is the count asymptotic to c times x for some constant c, or is it of higher order?

background.spoken: The claim is that the count S(x) grows faster than x times any fixed power of log x, so the linear asymptotic fails in the higher-order direction. The construction starts from three integers with the same abundancy index, reduces the identity to two equations in six primes lying on a split quadric, parametrises the quadric rationally, and counts prime points on the resulting planes with a sieve and a higher-dimensional Siegel–Walfisz theorem. The author notes that Guy's phrasing asks whether the count is cx + o(x) or of higher order, so a precise asymptotic is not required.
